responses.answer_text: At a point the derivative basically tells us how steep the curve is right there, its the slope of the tangent line drawn at that point.

If we take two points on the curve and draw a line through them (secant), and then slide the second point closer and closer to the first, that line becomes the tangent, and its slope is the derivative.
Derivative at a point = instantaneous rate of change of y wrt x, geometrically it equals tan(theta) where theta is angle tangent makes with x axis.
Geometrically f'(a) is nothing but the gradient of the tangent to y=f(x) at x=a, we get it by shrinking the secant line PQ till Q merges into P.
Think of zooming into the curve near a point, eventually it looks like a straight line and that straight line's slope is what derivative gives us, so its like the instant slope.
In limit form we write f'(x) = lim h->0 [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h, and this limit is exactly the slope of chord AB as B tends to A, ie tangent slope.
The value of derivative at any point tells the rate at which function is changing at that exact instant, and this rate visually appears as the steepness of tangent line touching curve there.

So basically first you draw a secant through the point and a nearby point, find its slope, then keep moving the nearby point closer until it becomes the tangent line, that final slope is the derivative and it represents how fast y changes per unit x at that spot.
Derivative just means the new function we get after differentiating, it doesn't really have any geometric picture, its purely an algebraic operation like integration.
The derivative of f at a point is the slope of the line joining that point to the origin, we just calculate y/x basically.
Geometric meaning is simply the slope of secant line between two points on curve, we don't need any limit for that, secant slope itself is the derivative.

The discriminant is b squared minus 4ac, and its sign tells us what kind of roots we get from the quadratic formula. If it's positive we get two different real roots, if it's zero the two roots collapse into one repeated root, and if it's negative the square root becomes imaginary so we get complex roots.

Basically inside the quadratic formula there's a square root of b²-4ac, and whether that thing under the root is positive, zero or negative decides everything. Positive means real and unequal roots, zero means real and equal, negative means the roots come out complex since you can't take root of a negative number normally.

D = b² - 4ac is like the deciding factor because it sits under the square root in x = (-b ± √D)/2a. When D<0 the root is imaginary so roots are complex conjugates, when D=0 both roots are same value, and when D>0 we get two separate real answers.

Two distinct real roots happen when discriminant b²-4ac is greater than zero, a repeated real root happens at exactly zero, and complex roots happen when it's negative — this all comes from the ± √(b²-4ac) term in the formula turning imaginary when negative.

Independent events are when one happening doesn't change the chance of the other, so we just multiply P(A) and P(B) to get P(A∩B). Mutually exclusive is totally different, it means both events literally cannot happen together so P(A∩B)=0.

For mutually exclusive events, if A occurs then B simply cannot occur, like getting a 2 and a 5 on a single die roll. Independence is a separate idea about probabilities not influencing each other, P(A|B)=P(A) basically, and the intersection formula becomes a simple product.

I always remember it as: mutually exclusive = no overlap at all in the sample space, independent = knowing one event tells you nothing about the other. They're answering completely different questions honestly.

Mutually exclusive events share no common outcomes so their intersection probability is zero, that's the venn diagram with no overlapping circles. Independent events can definitely overlap, their probabilities just multiply because one doesn't affect the other's likelihood.

Two events being independent means P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B), it's about the events not influencing each other's probability at all. Mutually exclusive on the other hand is about them physically not being able to happen at once, giving P(A∩B) = 0.

Honestly the easiest way to think of it, mutually exclusive is like coin lands heads or tails, only one can happen ever. Independent is more like flipping two separate coins, each result doesn't care what the other one did.

If you're told A happened and that changes nothing about how likely B is, they're independent. But if A happening literally rules out B ever happening, that's mutually exclusive, and these two properties are actually opposite kinds of relationships.

Independence is a probability concept, P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), while mutual exclusivity is a set theory concept about the events having empty intersection. In fact if both events have nonzero probability they can never be both independent and mutually exclusive at the same time, since one forces P(A∩B)=0 and the other forces it to be a nonzero product.
Independent events and mutually exclusive events are basically the same thing, both just mean the two events have nothing to do with each other so we treat them the same in probability problems.
Mutually exclusive events are independent because since they can't occur together, one event happening has zero effect on the other one occurring, so they don't affect each other at all.
For independent events the rule is P(A∩B) = P(A) + P(B), you just add up their individual probabilities since neither one depends on the other happening first.
